Energy Stores.intro: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. Understanding the different types of energy store is the starting point for all of P1.
Energy Stores.mnemonic: "King George Can't Eat Nachos, Even Mildly" — Kinetic, Gravitational, Chemical, (thermal) Energy, Nuclear, Electrostatic, Magnetic — the 8 energy stores.

sections.title: Types of Energy Store
sections.text: Energy can be held in eight distinct stores; recognising these stores is the foundation of all energy analysis in GCSE Physics.
points: Kinetic — energy of moving objects; calculated using KE = ½mv²
Gravitational potential — energy due to height above ground; calculated using GPE = mgh
Elastic potential — energy stored in stretched or compressed objects such as springs
Chemical — energy stored in chemical bonds (food, fuel, batteries); released in reactions
Thermal — energy stored in the internal energy of a substance; increases with temperature
Nuclear — energy stored in atomic nuclei; released in fission or fusion reactions
Electrostatic — energy stored due to the positions of charged objects relative to each other
Magnetic — energy stored in magnetic fields; e.g. between poles of magnets

sections.title: Conservation of Energy
sections.text: The total energy in a closed system always remains constant — energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred.
points: Law of conservation — energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores
Closed system — no energy enters or leaves; total energy remains constant
Dissipation — in real systems, some energy always transfers to thermal store of surroundings
Practical example — a falling ball transfers GPE to KE; at impact, KE transfers to thermal and sound stores
Language matters — say 'energy is transferred FROM the chemical store TO the kinetic store', not 'energy changes'

callout.label: Law of Conservation
callout.text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another. The total energy always stays the same.

sections.title: KE and GPE Calculations
sections.text: Two key equations allow you to calculate energy in the kinetic and gravitational potential stores.
points: KE = ½mv² — KE in joules (J), mass m in kg, speed v in m/s
Example KE — a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s: KE = ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J
GPE = mgh — GPE in joules, mass m in kg, g = 10 N/kg, height h in metres
Example GPE — a 5 kg object raised 4 m: GPE = 5 × 10 × 4 = 200 J
Energy conservation link — if an object falls freely, the loss in GPE equals the gain in KE

keyTerms.def: A way in which energy is held — kinetic, gravitational, thermal, chemical, etc.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores
Energy stored in moving objects
Energy stored due to an object's height above a reference point; GPE = mgh
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring or elastic material
Energy held in the internal energy (vibration of particles) of a substance
Energy spreading out into surroundings as thermal energy, becoming less useful

examTips: Use precise language: 'energy is transferred FROM the chemical store TO the kinetic store' — not just 'energy changes'.
Name both the starting store and the ending store in energy transfer descriptions.
KE = ½mv² — remember to square the speed, not the mass. A common error is squaring the wrong value.
commonMistakes: Saying energy is 'used up' — energy is always conserved, just transferred to less useful stores (e.g. thermal).
Confusing energy stores with energy transfer pathways — stores are where energy is held; pathways are how it moves.
Forgetting to halve in the KE equation — KE = ½mv², not mv².
clozePassages: Energy can be stored in different ways. Kinetic energy is the energy an object has due to its motion. Gravitational potential energy is stored when an object is raised above the ground. Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of chemical substances such as food and fuels. Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed materials. Thermal energy is stored in the internal energy of a substance.

Energy is measured in joules (J). The kinetic energy of a moving object can be calculated using KE = ½mv², where m is mass in kg and v is speed in m/s. The gravitational potential energy stored in an object is given by GPE = mgh, where m is mass, g is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth), and h is height in metres. These equations allow energy calculations in a wide range of situations.

Energy is stored in a variety of stores and transferred between them. A falling ball transfers gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy. Burning fuel transfers chemical energy to thermal energy and light. A stretched spring stores elastic potential energy. A battery stores chemical energy and transfers it to electrical energy. Understanding energy stores and transfers is fundamental to understanding how machines and natural processes work.

Energy Transfer.intro: Energy is transferred between stores by four pathways: mechanically, electrically, by heating, and by radiation. Understanding these pathways is essential for P1.
Energy Transfer.mnemonic: "MEER" — Mechanical, Electrical, heating (thermal), Radiation — the four energy transfer pathways.

sections.title: Transfer Pathways
sections.text: Energy moves between stores via four specific pathways — it is important to name the pathway correctly, not just the stores.
points: Mechanically — by a force acting over a distance (work done); W = F × d in joules
Electrically — by an electric current carrying energy through a circuit
By heating — by conduction (solids), convection (fluids), or radiation (electromagnetic waves)
By radiation — electromagnetic waves transfer energy without a medium (e.g. infrared, light, microwaves)
Example — a kettle: electrical pathway transfers energy from chemical store (power station) to thermal store (water)

sections.title: Energy Diagrams
sections.text: Sankey diagrams visually represent energy inputs and outputs, making efficiency easy to assess at a glance.
points: Sankey diagrams — width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy it represents
Useful energy — arrow points in the intended direction (usually right)
Wasted energy — arrows branch off, usually downwards, representing thermal losses
Conservation — total width of output arrows must equal width of input arrow
Reading efficiency — wider the useful arrow relative to input, the more efficient the device

sections.title: Reducing Wasted Energy
sections.text: Wasted energy cannot be eliminated but can be reduced through engineering and design improvements.
points: Lubrication — oil or grease between moving surfaces reduces friction, cutting thermal waste
Thermal insulation — lagging on pipes and walls reduces heat transfer to surroundings
Streamlining — aerodynamic shapes reduce air resistance, cutting energy wasted overcoming drag
Regenerative braking — electric vehicles capture kinetic energy during braking and store it as electrical energy
LED lighting — transfers much more electrical energy to light than old filament bulbs

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred when a force moves an object: W = F × d (joules)
Diagram showing energy input, useful output and wasted energy
Energy spreading out into surroundings as thermal energy — becomes less useful
Transfer of thermal energy through a material by vibration of particles and (in metals) free electrons
Transfer of thermal energy through a fluid by the bulk movement of the fluid itself
Transfer of energy by infrared electromagnetic waves — does not require a medium
Energy transferred when a force acts through a distance — W = F × d

examTips: All energy eventually dissipates as thermal energy — it isn't 'lost', just less useful; state this in exam answers.
In Sankey diagrams: total width in = total width out (conservation of energy); use this to find missing values.
For work done questions: W = F × d; always check the units — force in N, distance in m, work in J.
commonMistakes: Saying wasted energy disappears — it is transferred to the thermal store of surroundings; never destroyed.
Confusing work done (mechanical transfer) with power (rate of energy transfer).
Drawing Sankey diagrams where output arrows are wider than the input — this violates conservation of energy.
clozePassages: Energy can be transferred by heating, by waves (including light and sound), by electrical work, or by mechanical work (force causing movement). Energy is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another. This is the law of conservation of energy. In any energy transfer, the total energy before equals the total energy after.

Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material by the vibration of particles. It is most effective in solids, especially metals where free electrons also carry energy. Convection is the transfer of thermal energy through fluids by the movement of the fluid itself — warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, creating a convection current. Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves and does not require a medium.

Energy is often transferred to the thermal store of the environment as wasted energy. In a car engine, chemical energy from fuel is transferred to kinetic energy but much is wasted as heat. In a light bulb, electrical energy is transferred to light but also to heat. This wasted energy dissipates into the environment and becomes less useful. Insulation reduces unwanted thermal energy transfers and improves the efficiency of energy systems.

Efficiency.intro: Efficiency measures how well a device transfers energy usefully. No device is 100% efficient — some energy is always wasted.
Efficiency.mnemonic: "Useful Output Over Total Input" — the efficiency fraction in plain English: useful ÷ total.

sections.title: Efficiency Formula
sections.text: Efficiency compares the useful energy output to the total energy input and can be expressed as a decimal or percentage.
points: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input — gives a decimal between 0 and 1
Percentage efficiency — multiply by 100 to express as a percentage (0% to 100%)
Example — a motor transfers 600 J of 800 J input usefully: efficiency = 600/800 = 0.75 (75%)
Wasted energy — total input − useful output = wasted energy (e.g. 800 − 600 = 200 J wasted)
Can also use power — efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (× 100 for percentage). Or: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.

sections.title: Improving Efficiency
sections.text: Efficiency can be improved by reducing the energy wasted at each transfer stage.
points: Lubrication — reduces friction between moving parts, cutting thermal energy waste
Thermal insulation — reduces heat loss through walls, pipes, and engine components
Regenerative braking — electric cars capture kinetic energy on braking, storing it in the battery
LED technology — LEDs are ~90% efficient; old filament bulbs only ~5% efficient
Better design — streamlining vehicles and using low-resistance conductors reduces wasted energy

sections.title: Efficiency in Context
sections.text: Understanding efficiency helps evaluate devices and energy systems, and underpins decisions about energy use.
points: Power stations — coal power stations ~35% efficient; combined cycle gas ~60% efficient
Electric motors — up to 95% efficient; far more efficient than internal combustion engines (~25%)
Human body — muscles convert chemical energy to kinetic energy at ~25% efficiency
Comparison — a device with efficiency 0.85 wastes 15% of input energy as thermal energy
Never 100% — the second law of thermodynamics means some energy always dissipates to thermal stores

keyTerms.def: The fraction of input energy that is transferred to useful output energy
Energy transferred in the desired way by a device
Energy transferred in an unwanted way — usually as thermal energy
The total energy supplied to a device
The energy produced by a device — split into useful and wasted portions
Applying oil or grease to reduce friction between moving surfaces, improving efficiency

examTips: Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal (0.75) or percentage (75%) — check what the question asks for.
Wasted energy = total input − useful output; use this to find missing values in multi-step questions.
An efficiency of 0.75 means 75% of energy is usefully transferred and 25% is wasted as thermal energy.
commonMistakes: Giving efficiency greater than 1 (or 100%) — this is physically impossible; check your calculation if this happens.
Forgetting to subtract wasted energy: useful = total − wasted, not total + wasted.
Using energy values in different units without converting — always check that J and J (or W and W) are used consistently.
clozePassages: Efficiency is a measure of how much useful energy is transferred compared to the total energy input. It is calculated as: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input (× 100%). Efficiency can also be calculated using power values. No machine can be more than 100% efficient because some energy is always wasted, usually as thermal energy due to friction or air resistance.

The efficiency of devices can be improved by reducing energy losses. Using lubricants reduces friction in moving parts. Better insulation reduces heat loss. LED lights are much more efficient than traditional filament bulbs — they transfer a higher percentage of electrical energy to useful light. Streamlining vehicles reduces air resistance and improves fuel efficiency. Modern power stations and appliances are designed to maximise efficiency.

A Sankey diagram shows the energy input and outputs of a device. The width of each arrow represents the amount of energy. The useful energy output is shown going in the intended direction, while wasted energy is shown going in other directions, usually downwards. Sankey diagrams make it easy to visualise energy efficiency and identify where energy is being wasted. The total width of output arrows equals the width of the input arrow, showing conservation of energy.

Specific Heat Capacity.intro: Specific heat capacity (SHC) measures how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C.
Specific Heat Capacity.mnemonic: "Queen Might Change Temperatures" — Q = mcΔT — the specific heat capacity equation letter by letter.
Specific Heat Capacity.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Specific Heat Capacity
Image coming soon

sections.title: The Formula
sections.text: The specific heat capacity equation links energy supplied, mass, SHC, and temperature change in a single expression.
points: Q = mcΔT — energy Q in joules (J), mass m in kg, specific heat capacity c in J/kg°C, temperature change ΔT in °C
Example 1 — heating 2 kg of water (c = 4200) by 10°C: Q = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84,000 J
Example 2 — find c: 6000 J heats 0.5 kg of copper by 30°C: c = 6000 ÷ (0.5 × 30) = 400 J/kg°C
ΔT — means change in temperature = final temperature − initial temperature
Rearrangements — m = Q ÷ (cΔT); c = Q ÷ (mΔT); ΔT = Q ÷ (mc)

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Q = mcΔT — where Q = energy (J), m = mass (kg), c = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C), ΔT = temperature change (°C).

sections.title: What SHC Means
sections.text: SHC values tell us how much energy a material stores per kilogram per degree — high SHC means slow to heat and cool.
points: High SHC — needs lots of energy to heat up, releases lots when cooling; e.g. water = 4200 J/kg°C
Low SHC — heats up quickly with less energy; e.g. copper = 390 J/kg°C, aluminium = 900 J/kg°C
Water's high SHC — explains why the sea moderates coastal climates and why it is used in cooling systems
Central heating — water used in radiators because high SHC means it carries a large amount of thermal energy per kg
Storage heaters — use concrete or brick (high SHC) to store heat overnight and release during day

sections.title: SHC Experiment
sections.text: The SHC of a solid or liquid can be measured using an electrical heater and thermometer in a controlled experiment.
points: Setup — known mass of material in an insulated container; immersion heater connected to a joulemeter
Measurement — record energy supplied (Q from joulemeter) and temperature rise (ΔT from thermometer)
Calculate c — c = Q ÷ (mΔT) using the measured values
Sources of error — energy lost to surroundings makes measured c higher than the true value
Improvement — wrap sample in insulation; use a lid; allow time for temperature to equilibrate

keyTerms.def: Energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (J/kg°C)
The energy needed to raise an object's temperature by 1°C
The difference between final and initial temperature — used in Q = mcΔT
Total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a substance — increases with temperature
Instrument that measures the total electrical energy supplied to a device in joules
The energy held in a substance due to the temperature and mass of its particles

examTips: Q = mcΔT — learn this formula and the units for each quantity; it appears in almost every P1 exam.
Water has the highest SHC of common substances (4200 J/kg°C) — explain why it is used in central heating and cooling systems.
In SHC experiments, the measured value is always higher than the true value due to energy loss to surroundings.
commonMistakes: Using temperature in Kelvin instead of °C for ΔT — the change is the same in either scale, but use °C consistently.
Forgetting that ΔT = final temperature − initial temperature, not just the final temperature.
Swapping m and c in calculations — keep track of which value is mass (kg) and which is specific heat capacity (J/kg°C).
clozePassages: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1°C. It is measured in J/kg°C. The equation is: energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change (E = mc∆T). Water has a very high specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg°C, which is why it is used as a coolant and why the sea heats up and cools down slowly.

Materials with a high specific heat capacity need more energy to heat up and release more energy when they cool down. This makes them good for storing thermal energy. Water is used in central heating systems because its high specific heat capacity means it can carry a lot of energy. Concrete and stone also have relatively high specific heat capacities, which is why buildings made of these materials stay warm longer after heating.

Specific heat capacity experiments involve heating a known mass of a substance by a measured amount of electrical energy. A thermometer records the temperature change. Using the equation E = mc∆T, the specific heat capacity can be calculated. In practice, values are higher than theoretical ones because some energy is transferred to the surroundings rather than to the sample. Using insulation around the sample reduces this error.

Energy Resources.intro: Energy resources are used to generate electricity and heat. Understanding the advantages and disadvantages of renewable and non-renewable sources is essential for P1.
Energy Resources.mnemonic: "Never Run, Get Tired; Swim, Wave, Go Biking" — Nuclear, (coal/oil/gas) Renewable: Geothermal, Tidal, Solar, Wind, hydroelectric (Go), Biomass — all energy sources.

sections.title: Non-Renewable Resources
sections.text: Fossil fuels and nuclear fuels provide reliable, high-output power but are finite and have significant environmental costs.
points: Fossil fuels — coal, oil, natural gas; burn to produce steam → turbine → generator
Nuclear — uranium/plutonium fission heats water → steam → turbine; no CO₂ but produces radioactive waste
Reliable — can generate power on demand, regardless of weather; suitable as base-load power
High output — concentrated energy; small mass of fuel produces large amounts of electricity
Disadvantages — finite (will run out), CO₂ emissions (fossil fuels), radioactive waste (nuclear), pollution

sections.title: Renewable Resources
sections.text: Renewable energy sources are replenished naturally and produce little or no pollution, but many are intermittent.
points: Solar — PV cells convert light to electricity; solar thermal systems heat water directly
Wind — turbines turned by wind; no fuel costs; best offshore where wind is stronger
Hydroelectric — falling water drives turbines; very reliable; requires dam construction (habitat impact)
Tidal — tidal barrages or stream turbines; predictable but limited suitable locations
Wave — wave motion drives generators; variable and technology still developing
Geothermal — heat from Earth used to produce steam; continuous supply; limited to volcanic regions
Biomass — burning biological material (wood, crops); considered carbon neutral over lifecycle

sections.title: Comparing Energy Sources
sections.text: Choosing energy sources involves balancing reliability, cost, environmental impact, land use, and energy security.
points: Intermittency — wind and solar are only available when conditions are right; cannot guarantee supply
Land use — wind farms and solar farms require large areas; hydroelectric dams flood valleys
Carbon emissions — fossil fuels produce most CO₂; nuclear, wind, solar produce very little in operation
Start-up time — gas power stations start quickly (useful for peak demand); nuclear is slow to start
Cost — renewables have high installation cost but very low running costs; fossil fuels have ongoing fuel costs

callout.label: Key Comparison
callout.text: Non-renewable: reliable but polluting and finite. Renewable: clean and sustainable but often intermittent (not always available on demand).

keyTerms.def: An energy resource that will run out and cannot be replenished
An energy resource that will not run out and is naturally replenished
Device that converts kinetic energy of steam or water into rotational energy
Device that converts rotational kinetic energy into electrical energy
Not continuously available — wind and solar power are intermittent as they depend on weather
A process that does not add net CO₂ to the atmosphere over its lifecycle
The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity at high voltage across the UK

examTips: Most power stations work the same way: fuel heats water → steam → turbine → generator (except solar PV, wind turbines, and hydroelectric).
Renewable ≠ always available. Wind and solar are intermittent — this is a key limitation to mention in evaluation answers.
Be able to evaluate energy sources for 6-mark questions — consider reliability, cost, environment, land use, and energy security.
commonMistakes: Saying nuclear is renewable — it uses uranium which is a finite resource; it is non-renewable but low carbon.
Saying biomass produces no CO₂ — it does produce CO₂ when burned, but the carbon was recently absorbed from the atmosphere during growth.
Forgetting that hydroelectric has environmental impacts — flooding valleys and disrupting river ecosystems.
clozePassages: Fossil fuels — coal, oil, and natural gas — are non-renewable energy resources formed over millions of years. They release stored chemical energy when burned, producing carbon dioxide and contributing to climate change. Nuclear fuel is also non-renewable. Renewable resources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal, and biofuel. Renewable resources will not run out because they are replenished naturally.

Renewable energy sources have significant advantages — they produce little or no carbon dioxide and will not run out. However, they have drawbacks. Solar panels and wind turbines only generate electricity when the sun shines or wind blows, making supply unreliable. Hydroelectric dams flood valleys and disrupt ecosystems. Biomass burning releases carbon dioxide, though this is balanced by absorption during growth. Energy storage solutions are needed to balance supply and demand.

The UK generates electricity from a mix of energy sources. Electricity is generated in power stations by driving turbines connected to generators. In a fossil fuel power station, burning fuel heats water to make steam which drives the turbine. In a nuclear power station, nuclear reactions produce heat. Wind turbines are driven directly by wind. The National Grid distributes electricity at high voltage to reduce energy losses in transmission.
